items.title: Vincent Pelote interviewed by Monk Rowe, Orlando, Florida, February 25, 2017
items.q: I knew him. I used to meet him in New York with Ed Berger, we used to go see him play, and he would come and talk to me at the table.

ctx.x: A nice man. I knew him. I used to meet him in New York with Ed Berger, we used to go see him play, and he would come and talk to me at the table. Always asked me about my brother. I thought it was so funny, he met my brother maybe twice and every time he saw me he asked me, “How’s your brother doing.” And I was so touched by that. And another musician who wouldn’t mention Benny because he had a run-in with Benny Goodman was George Duvivier. Like also I met him, and what he would do is he would always call Benny…

Wow. You know what I loved about Joe and I noticed it with Milt Hinton and other fellows of that generation is they were such gentlemen, they were so nice, but at the same time if you disrespected them, like in a business fashion or — I witnessed this like a couple of times. Someone suggesting that they weren’t living up to their obligations. They took the heat and they were wait a minute, don’t besmirch my professionalism. And it was really good to witness that. You can be a nice guy and also stand up for your —

I saw it with Benny Carter also. He played a club in New York, Carlos #1 I guess it was. It was a club that was on Sixth Avenue. And he insisted on being paid in cash. And the guy said he would, the owner of the club said he would. And the guy was going to go back on that after Benny had played. And Benny insisted, “You give me my cash, this is what we agreed on — you don’t give me my cash you know —.” I don’t know what the consequences would have been but it was quite obvious that he was making Benny very angry.…
